Landlord: plays alone against the other two, takes the kitty and leads first. A landlord banks their own score.
Peasant: one of the two players against the landlord. Their scores go into the Commons.

Audit: a check of one claim on the Commons. Each claim rolls a die. A 1 means an audit. With an informer in the village, so does a 2. A claim caught above its fair share is cut back to it, and adds Denunciation.
Resentment: what the village holds against your private gains. Villagers play harder against you as it rises, and it adds Denunciation when a Quota ends.
Denunciation: the case building against you. Private purchases, caught lies and Resentment raise it. If it fills, the run ends.

Famine: the village's hunger. It rises for a missed Quota, for a Commons too small for what was claimed, and for each Quota past 3 in a row without the landlord's seat: by 1, then 2, 3 and at most 4. If it fills, the run ends.

That winter the households met after dark and divided the brigade's land between them. They marked the paper with thumbprints and seals. The next harvest was the largest the village had brought in, and the report to the commune did not say why. The paper also said who would raise the leaders' children if the leaders were taken away.

Nobody divided the land. The households farmed it together for eight years, split what there was, and wrote down true figures. Some years that was enough. The {surname} family ended the eighth year owning what it had owned in the first.

The {surname} family gave to the Commons every year and took what was handed back. In the eighth winter the granary was swept to the boards before the solstice. The brigade cut the ration twice more before spring.

In the eighth year the {surname} name went up on the wall outside the brigade office. The family kept its house and its place in the fields. The label went into the household register, under every name in the family.

By the eighth year the {surname} family held the land and the village ate. Rent came due after harvest and was paid in grain. People took off their caps at the gate. They called the {surname} family landlord, which was what they had called the last family to hold the land.
The {surname} storehouse was full in the eighth winter. It had two locks and a man paid to sleep against the door. Nothing left it before spring.

In the eighth year the village came to the {surname} gate together. They carried the ledgers out and read from them in the square. Every household still in the village was called on to speak. The land was divided again by autumn, and the {surname} family was given the share furthest from the well.
The village ran out of grain in Year {year}. The {surname} household was not on the next roll.
